rounds.name: Online Assessment Round
rounds.description: The online assessment comprised 70 questions to be completed in 90 minutes. It was conducted via Google Forms at the college premises. The marking scheme awarded +1 for each correct answer and imposed a -0.25 penalty for incorrect ones. The test was divided into four major sections: Java, Python, SQL, and Aptitude. Personally, I found the Aptitude section to be the most time-consuming. Unfortunately, I had less time left for it since I spent most of my time working through the first three sections.

rounds.name: Technical Round 1
rounds.description: I was the first candidate to be interviewed in my panel, and my interview took place from 1:15 - 2:05 PM. It began with my introduction, followed by an in-depth discussion about my resume. The questions covered my education, professional experience (internship), projects, and my interest in hackathons. The interviewer was polite and seemed genuinely interested in my projects and my Data Science degree from IIT Madras. This part lasted about 15–20 minutes. Next came the coding round. I was given a database schema and asked three SQL questions based on it. The first two questions were easy, similar to this question: Average Selling Price, while the third was of medium difficulty similar to this question: Monthly Transactions 1. The topics included aggregate functions, joins, and subqueries. I’d recommend practicing the “Top 50 SQL Questions” from LeetCode for such rounds. After that, the Data Science/Python coding round began. The interviewer provided a CSV file and asked me to use any notebook platform (Google Colab, Kaggle, or Jupyter Notebook). The questions were based on Pandas and NumPy, and I was asked to: Comment on the data quality (e.g., detecting anomalies like invalid syntax in the email column or negative salaries). Suggest how to remove or replace such data. Towards the end, the interviewer asked how I would travel if I got the opportunity and also inquired about my family background. I was able to answer all the questions confidently, explaining each concept in detail. Since I hadn’t faked anything in my resume, discussing my projects and experiences in depth felt natural and rewarding.

rounds.name: HR Round
rounds.description: Since I was the first to be interviewed in my panel, I had to wait quite a while for the results. My HR round selection was announced only around 6:00 PM, which meant there were about four long, uneventful hours in between. That wait honestly felt like the most boring part of the day. In both my technical and HR rounds, the interviewers showed a lot of interest in my Data Science degree from IIT Madras. The HR round itself was a classic one, focused more on understanding me as a person, my aspirations, and how I saw my future with the company. The tone was conversational, and the interviewer seemed genuinely curious about my career direction and motivations. It was less about testing technical knowledge and more about seeing whether I would be a good cultural and long-term fit for the organization.

questions.text: What are your future growth plans?

tips.text: My first interview was for an SDE role at WorkIndia. I cleared all rounds and interviews, making no mistakes from my side, answering all questions, and solving all the given DSA questions in an optimized way, yet I was still not selected for the HR round. The thing I learned is that placement remains a game of luck given that you have all the skills.

Tailor your resume according to the job description of the company, and make sure to include all the skills and projects relevant to the role you’re applying for. Check for grammatical errors, as they can instantly create a bad impression. Also, check your ATS score online (websites like Enhancv and Resume Worded can help). Most importantly, never fake information in your resume, if you’re caught, it leaves a lasting negative impression. Be true and genuine.
Always attend the PPT, as information such as the company’s values or history shared during it is often asked in the HR round.

If you have consistently worked hard for your placements from the start, then even with some hard luck, you will eventually end up with a good placement. Just don’t give up, keep trying and believe in the work you’ve put in so far.
I have always loved participating in hackathons, and I would highly recommend you take part in such coding competitions to continuously learn and grow your skills.

Focus on basic concepts, practice DSA regularly, as it requires consistency. Revise DBMS theory and SQL questions (especially the Top 50 SQL questions from LeetCode), review OS and CN, and try to learn Java, as it is required by many companies.

Whenever you learn new skills, make sure to first understand the basics and build a strong foundation. For example, if you’re interested in machine learning, start with linear algebra and statistics, and try to understand each algorithm mathematically, you’ll enjoy it even more.

Try to make open-source contributions and participate in events like Hacktoberfest, GSoC, etc. For that, your skills are your weapon, build strong foundations in whatever you are learning, and then collaborate with other developers online to expand your connections.

tips.text: Always tailor your resume to align with the specific job description of the role you're applying for.

Ensure that your resume maintains visual and structural consistency. Avoid mixing date formats, bullet styles, or using bold/italic formatting inconsistently across sections. A clean, well-organized resume gives a strong first impression.
Once your resume is finalized, evaluate its compatibility with Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS). Tools like Resume Worded can help — aim for a score of 65 or above.

The information shared during Pre-Placement Talks is extremely valuable, so it's important to be attentive — not just to the content of the presentation, but also to the names and roles of the presenters.

I made it a point to take multiple screenshots and jot down the specific examples used while the speaker explained some of the company's financial services. These details often come in handy during interviews.

While it's a good idea to ask thoughtful questions at the end of the session, it's even smarter to hold back a few insightful ones. Save them for your interview — this gives you an opportunity to show continued curiosity and engagement with the company during later stages.
Keep your technical concepts in Java and Python fresh, practice aptitude regularly to build speed, and remain calm under pressure.
Time constraints will challenge everyone equally—focus on accuracy, avoid panic, and read questions carefully.
make sure to eat at least a little and not be completely empty stomach due to stress/tension.
Even if your interview gets scheduled late, don’t worry and do your best.
Even if you don’t know something don’t stay completely silent and keep processing your thoughts out and don’t panic.
Your personality and confidence also matters, try to work on soft skills and effective communication.
Give as much mock interviews as you can to better prepare yourself.
Do not lie on your Resume but you can smartly change phrases so that your resume looks good.
Do not throw the sheets/papers in which you did your OA questions. They can be asked in an interview.
Make sure if you are adding any links then they are clickable in your resume
Prepare well around your resume projects & its tech stack. You can ask your friend to keep on cross questioning you on them
Prepare a couple of scenarios (even if fake) about disagreement in the team, or any times that you have shown leadership/ team spirit. These questions are very common too.
If you don’t know the answer or you are not able to recall it, try to put it across politely instead of saying something wrong
Think out loud when solving a DSA problem/ SQL query but when saying a theory answer try to sort of structure it in your mind first. Make use of technical terms & examples where possible
Maintain Eye Contact Ensure steady, natural eye contact with the interviewer. It shows confidence and helps build a connection, but avoid staring as it may come across as forced.
Be Mindful of What You Share Avoid oversharing personal experiences that don’t directly address the question. Focus on relevant, concise answers that highlight your suitability for the role.
Use the STAR Method Structure your answers to behavioral questions using the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result). It provides clarity and demonstrates a problem-solving mindset.
Show Respect in All Responses Be polite and professional. Even casual or off-topic comments should be delivered respectfully to avoid unintentionally offending the interviewer.
Frame Strengths and Weaknesses as Narratives Share your strengths and weaknesses with context. Use short stories or examples (real or carefully crafted) that showcase growth and self-awareness.
Avoid Monologues Don’t treat your answers like speeches. Keep the conversation balanced, concise, and interactive. Know when to stop and where to elaborate.
Display Confidence and Personality Strong communication and soft skills often outweigh technical skills in HR rounds. Let your personality come through—be confident, composed, and clear.
Always be Positive Always answer all questions in a positive manner and I’ll suggest don’t ask for feedback in an HR interview, you can in a technical round if you feel that you’ve done great.

Always Deny plans for Higher Studies Never show interest or accidently hint your passion for academia and research. Prepare solid reasons to justify why you’re choosing industry over academia, or it may become your reason for rejection.

do not lose hope if you are not selected, keep on trying !
